name: Workato
tagline: Enterprise integration, workflow automation, governance, and connectors

pricing.notes: The pricing model is not safely comparable as one fixed monthly USD amount. Review the official source before publication.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: 50,000 credits granted once; platform capability broadly matches self-service Pro until the one-time grant is exhausted.
tiers.notes: The 50,000 credits do not replenish monthly.

tiers.name: Enterprise Standard
tiers.limits: Custom platform edition, usage allowance, users and governance.
tiers.notes: Quote combines a platform fee and usage.

tiers.name: Enterprise Business
tiers.limits: Custom higher-scale platform edition, usage and governance.

tiers.name: Enterprise
tiers.limits: Custom enterprise-scale integrations, usage, security and support.

tiers.name: Workato One
tiers.limits: Custom enterprise orchestration and agentic-work platform scope.

pricing.freeTierCaps: 50,000 one-time credits; they do not refresh monthly
pricing.billingTerms: self-service Pro is monthly only; enterprise contracts are custom and typically combine platform-edition and usage fees
pricing.hiddenCosts: Unused self-service credits expire each month. Tasks, API operations, rows and Genie or AI work can consume credits; successful steps in a recipe that later fails may still count, and reruns consume credits again.

verdictSummary: Do not mistake the interface for the product. Workato's durable value is connectors, auth, reliability, which a solo one-shot build cannot reproduce responsibly. The prompt therefore builds only the closest honest personal consolation tool.
coreLoopDIY: Build one explicit enterprise automation workflow with a trigger, validated steps, retries, logs, and a manual replay button.
diyTimeEstimate: not a true replacement; consolation build in one to two days
replacementScope: consolation build only; the paid product's moat remains
requirements: API credentials for the two chosen services
Explicit README warning that this is a consolation build, not a production replacement
whatYouLose: schema drift handling and enterprise controls
whyPeopleStillPay: Workato: One automation is easy. Subscribers pay for maintained integrations, credentials, retries, observability, and someone else owning breakage.
ongoingBurden: Maintain OAuth, rate limits, webhooks, retries, queues, idempotency, logs, secret rotation, and third-party API changes.

priorArt.name: Activepieces
priorArt.desc: Open-source automation builder with connectors and self-hosting.

priorArt.name: n8n
priorArt.desc: Source-available workflow automation engine and connector reference.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Activepieces Community Edition
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Good automation, wrong governance tier: enterprise identity, audit, and controls still cost money.

rejectedAlternatives.name: n8n Community Edition
rejectedAlternatives.desc: A capable engine, but the free edition does not replace Workato's governance and connector support.

notes: Credibility row: Workato survives for a structural reason, not because its interface is difficult to copy.
prompt:
Build the closest honest consolation tool inspired by Workato; do not claim to replace its structural moat.
Use exactly this stack: Next.js 15 + TypeScript + PostgreSQL + BullMQ.
Primary job: Build one explicit enterprise automation workflow with a trigger, validated steps, retries, logs, and a manual replay button.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: schema drift handling and enterprise controls; hundreds of maintained connectors; OAuth app verification.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
